reason: The hypothesis makes specific claims about Q235 steel's native oxide composition, its room-temperature barrier properties, and its high-temperature failure mechanism, but the single cited passage (E1) discusses mass loss and elemental depletion in an FCC HEA versus 316H stainless steel in FLiBe salt, providing no evidence about Q235 steel, magnetite layers, or the proposed temperature-dependent barrier breakdown mechanism.
premises: Q235 steel in its as-received state has a native oxide layer predominantly composed of magnetite.
This native oxide layer acts as an effective barrier at room temperature, limiting further oxidation and mass loss.
At high temperatures (700–900 °C), thermal stresses and accelerated ion diffusion cause the oxide layer to crack, spall, or transform.
Breakdown of the oxide barrier in high-temperature aggressive salt environments leads to rapid substrate degradation and extensive mass loss.
The cited evidence (E1) supports the mechanism of protective layer breakdown leading to degradation in aggressive environments.
